1.pericope_label: At that time the LORD said unto me, Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first, and come up unto me into the mount, and make thee an ark of wood

schools.summary: Fix the occasion at the close of the second forty days, after the intercession, so that the order is itself a token of reconciliation; but deny that the notice of the ark stands in its proper place, since it belonged to the tabernacle, and refuse to require that things related together be referred to the same moment.

Sort the commands rather than the days — the ark ordered in the earlier period, the tables after the vision from the cleft of the rock and before the intercession — and reject Rashi's two arks while allowing that a temporary receptacle may have held the tables until Bezaleel's was finished.

Read the renewal of the broken tables as the surest evidence of reconciliation, and the division of labour as an order of grace: Moses hews the stone, God writes, because the law prepares a heart by conviction while only grace writes the law upon it. Ten words, not ten volumes, and a second edition needing no amendment.

debates.question: Can the events of this chapter be fitted to a single timeline?

sides.position: Yes, if the commands are sorted rather than the days: the ark ordered earlier, the tables after the vision from the rock
No — the order of the history is inverted, and it is exacting too much to require that things related together belong to the same moment
The order belongs to the close of the second forty days, after the intercession

debates.question: Who made the ark spoken of here?

sides.position: Moses began it as a plain chest and Bezaleel finished and overlaid it; or Moses ordered it made against his coming down
There were two arks, one for war and one for the tabernacle
No second ark; at most a temporary receptacle until Bezaleel's was finished

outliers.note: Alone allegorises the vessel, making the ark a figure of Christ in whom salvation is now kept safe, and alone turns "there they be" on his own hearers — God has entrusted us with Bibles and sabbaths, and there they be.
His block at this verse is the chapter argument and a bare cross-reference, with no exposition; excluded as carrier material.

2.pericope_label: And I will write on the tables the words that were in the first tables which thou brakest, and thou shalt put them in the ark; and I turned myself and came down from the mount, and put the tables in the ark which I had made; and there they be, as the LORD commanded me

schools.summary: Correct the common error that Moses wrote the law a second time, tracing it to a change of person in the Exodus narrative; deny any pluperfect in Hebrew, so that "the ark which I had made" is simply "which I made," meaning caused to be made; and read the stone tables as figures of the fleshy tables of the heart.

Draw two inferences from the sameness of the words — that they were God's and not Moses', and that no change had been made in them though the people had broken them, of which the breaking of the tables was itself a representation.
Take the rewriting as proof that God's wrath was turned away, and the writing of his law in our inward parts as the surest proof of reconciliation.

sides.position: God, not Moses; the contrary opinion rests on a change of person in the Exodus narrative

outliers.note: Alone builds a sustained typology from the two pairs of tables — the first answering to the heart of Adam, the second to the new covenant of the Spirit — and alone sets the two Pentecosts side by side as the day of the letter and the day of the Spirit.

6.pericope_label: And the children of Israel took their journey from Beeroth of the children of Jaakan to Mosera: there Aaron died, and there he was buried; and Eleazar his son ministered in the priest's office in his stead. From thence they journeyed unto Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbath, a land of rivers of waters

schools.summary: Deny that Moses intends an itinerary at all, since his object is only to mark where Aaron died; recognise in that death the punishment of the people's rebellion and in Eleazar's succession the sign of God's fatherly grace; and account for the divergent place-names by alternative names or by stations passed without encampment.

Read the passage as a parenthesis closed four verses later, inserted as evidence that the intercession was answered; and print at length Kennicott's case that these verses contradict the itinerary given elsewhere and are repaired by the Samaritan Pentateuch — remarks that should not be hastily rejected.

Refuse Knobel's contradiction by referring "at that time" not to the fortieth year but generally to the restoration of the covenant at Sinai, and read the separation of Levi as a manifestation of mercy toward Israel.

debates.question: Can the itinerary in these verses be reconciled with the complete catalogue of the march?

sides.position: No — the text as it stands contradicts itself on the order of stations and on where Aaron died; the Samaritan Pentateuch repairs it
The remarks should not be hastily rejected, though they are not endorsed
No itinerary is intended; Moses only marks where Aaron died, and the names may vary or the stations be passed without encampment
It is hard to say why these journeys are mentioned here at all

debates.question: Does "at that time" date the separation of Levi to Aaron's death?

sides.position: No — it refers generally to the restoration of the covenant at Sinai; the alleged contradiction fails
A contradiction with the other books stands
holders: Knobel (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: Later still, after the tabernacle was erected; what stands here may be a renewal

outliers.note: His block at this verse is only a pointer to Kennicott’s remarks, which the source files at the end of the chapter; the remarks treat these verses and were read here, where Clarke holds a key.

8.pericope_label: At that time the LORD separated the tribe of Levi, to bear the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to stand before the LORD to minister unto him, and to bless in his name; wherefore Levi hath no part nor inheritance with his brethren; the LORD is his inheritance. And I stayed in the mount, according to the first time, forty days and forty nights

schools.summary: Date the separation at Sinai rather than at Aaron's death, while noting that both events involve the loss of a territorial inheritance through bearing the burden of the law; and answer the critic who says Deuteronomy knows no distinction between priests and Levites by distributing the three duties between them after Rashi.

Ground the dignity of the tribe in God's authorship rather than its own merit, so that no one may overthrow the decree in pride; and give the practical reason for the lost inheritance, that a tribe kept at the sanctuary had no leisure to plough and sow.

Gloss standing before the Lord from its use of prophets and angels as the posture of a minister, define the portion concretely as tithes and offerings, and find in the command to lead the people a type of the one who intercedes and also commands.

debates.question: Does Deuteronomy distinguish priests from Levites?

sides.position: Yes — bearing the ark belongs to the Levites, ministering and blessing to the priests
The writer knows no such distinction
holders: a recent critic (as reported by Ellicott)

outliers.note: Alone reads the passage as a guard against rivalry, taking "unto this day" to look back over the instances in which God had shown favour to the Levites lest the dispute be reopened.

12.pericope_label: And now, Israel, what doth the LORD thy God require of thee, but to fear the LORD thy God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve the LORD thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul, to keep the commandments of the LORD, and his statutes, which I command thee this day for thy good?

schools.summary: Reduce the whole law to the two heads Christ named, love of God and love of neighbour, so that nothing is required for a good life but piety and justice; treat Paul's "soberly" as the seasoning of that life rather than a third ingredient, and explain that where only the second table is named, religion is being tested rather than buried.

Break the demand into four — fear, walk, love, serve — defining heart as the whole of the affections and soul as the will, understanding and judgment, and taking the requirement as duty and gratitude for amazing mercies.

Quote Rashi that after all their sin God asks nothing but fear, report the rabbinic maxim that everything is in Heaven's hand save the fear of Heaven, and set against it the promise that God will put his fear in men's hearts.

Hear the verse as an orator's appeal and answer it with the psalmist's question, what shall I render; then list the requirement in seven parts, adding that obedience is not merely rewarded but is itself the better condition, since meekness, sobriety and contentment are what make a man easy and safe and truly great.

debates.question: Is the fear of God within a man's own power?

sides.position: The rabbinic maxim says everything is in Heaven's hand to bestow except the fear of Heaven
Against it stands the promise that God will put his fear in their hearts

outliers.note: Alone uses the verse as the occasion for a summary of the whole law, and alone anticipates the objection that Paul adds a third term by making soberness the seasoning of a pious life rather than an ingredient.

14.pericope_label: Behold, the heaven and the heaven of heavens is the LORD's thy God, the earth also, with all that therein is. Only the LORD had a delight in thy fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them, even you above all people, as it is this day

schools.summary: Take the doubled phrase as exhausting the idea of heaven entirely, precisely so that the choice of one nation out of all may stand in contrast; and compress the election to a sentence — the whole world is the Lord's, and for all that he chose thy fathers.

Deny that Israel differed by personal dignity or excellence of race, press the Hebrew that says the Lord coveted to love their fathers as marking an inclination rather than a decision, and call it inestimable condescension that God should pass by heaven and earth to set his heart on a few obscure men.

Refuse the tidy threefold division of the heavens as explaining very little, and read the plurals as a statement of the sheer immensity of creation — systems beyond systems in endless gradation, every star a sun with its own attendant worlds.

debates.question: What do the plural heavens denote?

sides.position: Three ascending regions — atmosphere, planetary system, region of the blessed
Not that, which explains very little, but the sheer immensity of creation, systems beyond systems
The doubling simply exhausts the idea of heaven, for the sake of the contrast that follows

outliers.note: Alone reads the plural heavens cosmologically, with every star a sun attended by its own worlds and systems ascending in endless gradation to the throne of God.

16.pericope_label: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked. For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward: he doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger. Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt

schools.summary: Define circumcision of heart negatively as laying aside all insensibility to the love of God, and state the dependence flatly — without it neither true fear nor true love of God is possible; then read the Hebrew's second clause as consequence rather than command, and set God's might beside his care for the helpless.

Trace the sense from the rite's original purpose as a consecration separating Abraham's children from the heathen, require a returning love as the only fit answer to experienced grace, and explain the turn to the fatherless and the stranger by our readiness to injure the abject, whom God succours because he accepts no man's person.

Take the command as proof that the outward rite always pointed at the purification of the soul, and press the figure of the foreskin as the filthiness which leaves a man unclean if not cut away; on the titles that follow, dwell on the power from which all being proceeds.

debates.question: If circumcision of heart is God's work, why is it commanded?

sides.position: To bring men to a sense of their need of it and stir them to seek it from the God who alone can perform it
Because the command is at once a demand for returning love and a reproof of past obstinacy
Because the Hebrew reads as consequence — circumcise the heart, and ye will harden your neck no more

outliers.note: Alone quotes Rashi’s pairing of God’s might with his humility, and matches it with the psalm that sets the healing of the broken-hearted beside the numbering of the stars.

20.pericope_label: Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God; him shalt thou serve, and to him shalt thou cleave, and swear by his name. He is thy praise, and he is thy God, that hath done for thee these great and terrible things, which thine eyes have seen

schools.summary: Read the four verbs as one reverence shown three ways, in deed, in heart and with the mouth; recover the emphasis of the Hebrew word order, and quote Rashi that the permission to swear follows only when the other qualities are established.

Take the oath from God's side — eternal truth cannot be more grossly insulted than by being summoned as witness to a falsehood — and note that the heathen professed reverence in swearing while excusing deceit toward those they judged to deserve it. Read "thy praise" as warning: strip away that glory and nothing remains but shame.

Gloss cleaving as firm confidence, true affection and constant obedience; and turn the closing phrase on the reader, since it is an eternal honour to be in God's friendship, and strange that those who fear him should be ashamed to own it.

debates.question: How is swearing by God's name consistent with reverence?

sides.position: It is permitted only after fear, service and cleaving are established, so that the name is not profaned
The danger is perjury: eternal truth cannot be more grossly insulted than by being summoned as witness to a falsehood

outliers.note: His block at this verse expounds the prohibition of perjury from the law of holiness rather than this verse directly, and reaches it through Cicero and the Thyestes of the poets; it was used only for the clause on swearing, which it does bear upon.

22.pericope_label: Thy fathers went down into Egypt with threescore and ten persons; and now the LORD thy God hath made thee as the stars of heaven for multitude

schools.summary: Meet the difficulty of the rate of increase first from the promise, the multiplication being presented as divine rather than purely natural, and then from the genealogies of Chronicles, where one Simeonite had sixteen sons and six daughters while his brethren had few — modern calculations being perhaps not adequate to such a rate.
Fix the number as seventy in all, Jacob and his sons included, and read the multitude as the plain discharge of the promise that they should be as the stars of heaven.

Set the seventy against the six hundred thousand, note that all of those had themselves died within forty years save three men, and draw the moral that God can as easily diminish and bring low as increase and multiply.

debates.question: How is the rate of increase to be accounted for?

sides.position: As the fulfilment of a divine promise, and not purely natural — but the Chronicles genealogies show extraordinary natural rates too
As a display of the power that can as easily diminish and bring low
As the plain correspondence of the event to the promise made to Abraham

outliers.note: Alone answers the demographic objection from the genealogies of Chronicles, and alone concedes drily that modern calculations may not be adequate to such a rate of increase.
